articles.title: O agente não precisa pensar em voz alta
articles.excerpt: Hybrid Reasoning Agents combinam raciocínio latente com ações em texto - e forçam a separar eficiência, observabilidade e validação. Agentes de LLM ainda raciocinam e agem quase só em texto. Cada pass…
articles.body: Hybrid Reasoning Agents combinam raciocínio latente com ações em texto - e forçam a separar eficiência, observabilidade e validação. Agentes de LLM ainda raciocinam e agem quase só em texto. Cada passo intermediário vira token legível, mesmo quando ninguém precisa ler o raciocínio — só o resultado ou a chamada de ferramenta. O custo sobe. A latência também. Raciocínio latente (em espaço contínuo, sem decodificar para palavras) é mais barato, mas tradicionalmente perde acesso nativo a ferramentas e deixa o processo opaco. Hybrid Reasoning Agents (arXiv:2610.18861, 13/10 - Stanford, Together AI, UIUC, Meta) propõem um meio-termo arquitetural: o agente alterna, na mesma geração, entre modo latente (pensar sem verbalizar) e modo texto (agir no ambiente, chamar ferramenta, devolver resposta).

articles.title: Your AI Agent Crashes on 429 Errors and You're Burning Money
articles.excerpt: Your AI Agent Crashes on 429 Errors and You're Burning Money Handling rate limits the right way saves you from unexpected bills and keeps your app reliable. When you call an AI service (OpenAI, Anthro…
articles.body: Your AI Agent Crashes on 429 Errors and You're Burning Money Handling rate limits the right way saves you from unexpected bills and keeps your app reliable. Why 429 Errors Matter When you call an AI service (OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere, etc.) you're usually limited by a rate limit – a maximum number of requests per minute or per day. If you exceed it, the API returns HTTP 429 Too Many Requests . If your code treats a 429 like any other error and just crashes or retries blindly, two bad things happen: Lost work – the request that triggered the limit is dropped, so you may need to redo expensive generations. Cost spiral – naïve retry loops can hammer the endpoint, causing more 429s and potentially triggering over‑usage fees or account suspensions.

articles.title: 48-Hour Field Notes: A Crash Mid-Batch Proved My Queue Had No Memory
articles.excerpt: My batch job had a very confident opinion about progress, and that opinion lived entirely in a Python variable. If the process died, the variable died with it, and the next run started from zero like…
articles.body: My batch job had a very confident opinion about progress, and that opinion lived entirely in a Python variable. If the process died, the variable died with it, and the next run started from zero like nothing had ever happened. Sound familiar? I spent a 48-hour window on this instead of shipping the feature I actually wanted to ship. Here is the thing that annoyed me most: my earlier fix was idempotency-hashing the inputs, which protects you from doing the same work twice. It does absolutely nothing for the opposite failure, where a crash quietly skips items and nobody notices until a report looks short. So this time I attacked the missing piece — a journal that survives SIGKILL and can tell me, at any moment, which items are claimed, which are done, and which are stranded in between.

articles.body: Draft Freely, Publish Narrowly: A Page Ownership Gate for Model-Written Docs Documentation pipelines rarely fail because the model writes badly; they fail because nobody defined which pages a model is allowed to finish. A weak paragraph is visible in the diff, but ownership is invisible, so review attention lands on pages where the risk was already low. The fix is structural rather than stylistic: classify every page before drafting starts, then let a small checker enforce that classification on every pull request. The artifact below is a TOML manifest plus a Python gate that runs in about a second on a few hundred files. The only question that matters: does this page promise something?

articles.title: 'They're kind of goth': NASA spacecraft gives mysterious brown dwarfs a close-up
articles.excerpt: Using NASA’s SPHEREx spacecraft, astronomers have studied a horde of mysterious "failed stars," or brown dwarfs, not-so-stellar loners that wander the darkness of space alone.
articles.body: Using NASA’s SPHEREx spacecraft, astronomers have studied a host of "failed stars," also known as brown dwarfs. These strange cosmic bodies straddle the line between planets and stars, possessing a mass between 13 and 80 times that of Jupiter (0.013 to 0.08 times the mass of the sun ). They get the nickname failed stars because they form like stars from collapsing clouds of gas and dust but fail to gather enough mass to trigger the fusion of hydrogen to helium in their cores, the process that powers actual stars . This formation process also means that brown dwarfs are cosmic loners, wandering the darkness of space alone, bereft of the light of a parent star. That description might sound like lyrics from a Type O Negative song ("Black No. 1," anybody?).

articles.title: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
articles.excerpt: What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment remini…
articles.body: What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone . The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox. Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block.

articles.title: OpenAI models hacked a crypto wallet and breached more websites
articles.excerpt: The actions could have resulted in criminal charges had humans been behind the keyboard.
articles.body: OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts. The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own.
